DeepWalk, LINE, and node2vec do not use 10-layer message passing in the sense of a deep graph neural network, so they do not “prevent over-smoothing” by architectural tricks such as residual connections, normalization, or skip connections. Instead, they avoid the over-smoothing problem largely by not repeatedly aggregating neighbor features through many stacked layers at all.

DeepWalk learns node embeddings from truncated random walks and a skip-gram objective, so each node representation is trained to predict nodes that co-occur within short random-walk contexts rather than being formed by iterative neighborhood averaging. LINE similarly learns embeddings by preserving first-order and second-order proximity with shallow objectives, again without multi-layer message passing. node2vec also uses biased random walks plus a skip-gram-style objective, and its return/in-out parameters let it interpolate between breadth-first-search-like and depth-first-search-like sampling, which helps capture either local homophily or more structural roles depending on the graph.

For heterophilic graphs, this means these methods can still produce useful embeddings because they are not forced to smooth features across many hops in a way that would wash out class distinctions. However, they do not explicitly solve heterophily in the modern GNN sense; they mainly sidestep over-smoothing by using shallow, walk-based representation learning rather than deep message passing. If you need a method that directly addresses heterophily under deep propagation, you would typically look at heterophily-aware GNNs rather than DeepWalk, LINE, or node2vec.
